body: At about half past nine at a wedding reception in a village hall, the disco cuts out. Not dramatically — a plug, a look, a young man crouching behind a speaker with a torch on his phone. There is that flat couple of minutes where everybody can suddenly hear each other and nobody knows what to do with their hands. Then an aunt of the bride, sixty-one and two glasses of wine in, starts a chorus from a church hall in about 1971. Half the room has it by the third word. Stranger still are the arms: people who have not thought about that song in forty years are doing the actions, in time, laughing at themselves for it, and not stopping.

Nobody in that hall had revised. There was no cue and no words on a screen, and most of them could not tell you a single thing they were taught in that same hall on those same mornings. The tune came back complete, and it brought the body with it.

Almost everybody can produce, on demand, a song they learned before they were twelve. Not a sermon from that period. Not a lesson, and usually not a verse. A song — whole, with the tune, and very often with the actions.

It is worth taking the word still seriously, because it is doing more work than it looks. You did not maintain that song. You never rehearsed it, never revisited it, and would have said honestly that you had forgotten it. Nothing else from that age survives that way: not the times tables, not the address of a house you lived in for six years, not the names of most of the people in the photograph. But the thing set to a melody, with a metre holding the syllables in place, was not stored the way information is stored. It was installed. Music binds to memory in a manner ordinary speech does not, and childhood is when that binding is strongest and very nearly permanent.

Which is why the children’s frequencies on this band are not an afterthought at the end of it. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today, and the children’s stations sit together in the low three hundred and sixties with numbers of their own.

Holding them to the same standard as everything else on the dial costs more than treating them as the simple end of it, and it is done deliberately. A children’s song here stands on a passage exactly as a five-minute worship track does, and carries the same permanent identifier, so what it teaches can be checked by anybody who cares to look. That is not fussiness about a nursery format. Whatever is put into a child in song is still going to be in there in fifty years, and that is not a small responsibility.

The culture has gone the other way, and quickly. Children’s audio has become almost purely a pacifier: something to keep the back seat quiet between here and Grandma’s, chosen by whatever is loudest and most colourful, served by a recommendation engine tuned to keep a four-year-old watching. Nobody involved is wicked. The question being optimised is simply how long the child stays engaged, and no system in that chain is asking what the child will still be able to sing at sixty. So the most permanent shelf in human memory is being filled, at scale, by whatever happens to be in front of it.

So the band groups those frequencies where a hand finds them without looking, which matters more than it sounds. A parent in a car with a crying child is not browsing. They need to land on something safe in one movement, with no menu, and know exactly what is going to come out of the speakers. That is the ordinary competence of a real dial, and the reason the children’s numbers are neighbours rather than scattered.
This is not an argument against teaching children properly. It is a question about what remains when the teaching has gone.

Be fair to the lesson first. A song cannot define a term, handle a question from a bright nine-year-old, or correct an error out loud, and a childhood of choruses without any teaching produces adults with a great deal of religious feeling and no furniture to put it in. Catechism does real work. But ask almost any believer what they can say from memory of what they were given as a child, and you will get the song. The lesson was carried in a container that leaks; the chorus in one that does not. Both were poured in on the same mornings, and only one is still there.
You do not remember what you were taught at eight. You remember what you sang.

A woman of thirty-eight is lying in an anaesthetic room with a cannula in the back of her hand, waiting, while two members of staff talk quietly about a rota by the door. It is a Thursday. She is not frightened exactly, but she has run out of things to think about, and the ceiling here is the kind with little holes in the tiles. What arrives, unbidden, is a chorus with hand actions from a church hall in 1996 — a song she would have described an hour earlier as long gone. She does not sing it. She goes through it twice in her head, actions and all. The anaesthetist starts counting. She does not get to the end of it a third time.
Nothing composed and adult came. Nothing she had learned since she was old enough to choose what she believed came either. What came was the thing that had been set to a tune and put in a child.

It cuts both ways, and the risk has to be stated as plainly as the strength. Whatever is put in is what will still be in there, including the parts that were wrong. A sentimental half-truth with a good tune settles every bit as deep as a true line and is far harder to shift later, since a five-year-old has no way at all to weigh what a song is asserting. Songs teaching small children that God is pleased with them when they are good have done a great deal of quiet damage in exactly that way.

Which is why the answer is care rather than avoidance. Nothing this strong gets safer by being handed to whoever was cheapest to commission; it gets safer when somebody will say what each song stands on and let it be checked. That is why these frequencies are hosted and scheduled rather than shuffled — somebody is answerable for what plays at four o’clock on a Tuesday, as somebody is answerable for what is said in a classroom. Not because children need protecting from music. Because they are about to keep it.

So the children’s end of this dial is not the easy end. It is the part of the band with the longest memory attached to it, and the only part where the work being done today will be answered for in the middle of the century by people who cannot presently tie their shoes. A children’s song is doctrine that will outlast almost anything else you manage to teach.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to build, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you have children in the house, begin at HM 360.30 — God’s Little Lambs. It is the gentler of the two children’s frequencies, built for ordinary hours rather than parties: the getting dressed, the tea, the twenty minutes before bed when everything has to come down a notch. This article has been arguing that what is set to a tune in childhood is what a person keeps, so the only serious question about a children’s station is what it is putting in. That one is put together on the assumption that the answer matters, and its songs stand on passages anybody is welcome to check. Have it on for a fortnight of ordinary mornings and you will hear the results coming back at you from the back seat.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an instruction, because no child has ever learned a chorus from a curriculum decision. Put HM 360.30 on tomorrow while the toast is going in, and then get on with your morning. You will not see it working, and that is normal — it did not look like anything when it was done to you either. Somewhere around the middle of this century, in a corridor or a car park or an anaesthetic room, somebody is going to need a sentence and find they already have one.
